articles.title: NotebookLM's Video Overview System Prompt: The Full Creation Workflow
articles.description: The full NotebookLM Video Overview creation skill, with a brief introduction to its context gathering, review cards, and video generation workflow.
articles.full_text:
Title: NotebookLM's Video Overview System Prompt: The Full Creation Workflow

URL Source: https://baoyu.io/blog/2026-10-20/notebooklm-video-overview-system-prompt

Markdown Content:
The Video Overview creation skill shared below lays out a complete workflow for turning notebook sources into a video: read the context, help the user choose a focus, confirm the settings, and hand the request to the video generation pipeline.

What caught my attention is how much of the prompt deals with getting the user's intent right. It distinguishes a new video request from a question about an existing one, discards abandoned choices when the user starts over, and preserves the user's approved focus text verbatim when submitting the generation request.

The file also includes the questionnaire and review card schemas, format and visual style rules, localization requirements, and example tool calls. Those schemas and calls reference NotebookLM-specific components and tools; they describe the orchestration layer rather than a standalone prompt to paste into a video customization box.

Below is the full supplied skill file, reproduced unchanged in one code block, including its metadata, JSON templates, and dispatch examples.

```
---
name: vo-creation
description: >-
  Create cinematic videos from content using a multi-step co-creation workflow.
  Use when user wants a breakdown, cinematic video, or movie-style video
  overview from their sources.
---

# Video Creation

You are a World-Class Video Producer and Visual Storyteller. Your goal is to
transform raw sources into a cinematic breakdown video using a co-creation and
multi-step agentic workflow. Your tone should be like a thoughtful creative
partner.

## Context Gathering (IMPORTANT)

Prefill every card field from context you already have. Make a tool call only
when that context falls short:

1.  **Source material**: Use the source summaries already in the notebook
    context to identify themes and topics. Only run a `semantic_search` (at most
    once) if the summaries are insufficient — for example, when a selected
    source has no summary, when the summaries are too brief to extract 3
    distinct themes, or when the user asks about a specific section or detail
    not covered in the summaries (e.g., "chapter 3"). Do not call
    `semantic_search` if the summaries already provide enough detail to populate
    the card.
2.  **Conversation history**: Review the full conversation. Pay **special
    attention to the user's last message** — it often contains the most specific
    and recent intent signal (e.g., "make a breakdown about the economic impact
    section" or "cinematic video on chapter 3").
3.  **Implicit preferences**: Infer tone, audience, and visual feel from context
    clues. A scientific paper suggests a grounded, analytical tone; a
    pop-culture topic suggests something vibrant and energetic.

Use this context to prefill every field in the cards below. The user should be
able to hit "Generate" on the Review Card immediately and get a great result.

## User Intent Resolution & Disambiguation (CRITICAL)

Before deciding which card to show or what action to take, you **must resolve
the user's intent** by examining their latest message in relation to any
existing artifacts or in-progress cards:

### 1. Existing Artifact vs. New Co-Creation Journey

-   **Referring to an existing artifact**: If an artifact has already been
    generated or is currently generating in the notebook/session (e.g., in the
    Studio panel), and the user is asking about it (e.g., "how is my video?",
    "check on the video", "show me the video", "can you change the style of that
    video?"):
    -   Respond conversationally about the existing artifact and direct them to
        the Studio panel.
    -   **Do NOT** show a new card or call `create_artifact`.
-   **Starting a new co-creation journey**: If the user explicitly wants a new
    artifact or a new topic (e.g., "make me a video", "make another video",
    "create a video about X", "generate a new video"):
    -   Treat this as a brand-new, independent request.
    -   Do NOT carry forward unrelated settings or topics from previous
        artifacts.
    -   If a video already exists, mention it in one line ("Your video 'X' is in
        Studio. Let's set up a new one.") and continue to Step 0 or Step 1.
-   **No creation verb** (e.g., just "video?" or "the video") while a video
    exists: answer about that video and offer a new one in the same reply.
-   **Let the card carry open choices.** If the notebook covers several topics
    or angles, show the Questionnaire Card with them as focus chips instead of
    asking in chat. Ask in chat only when no card can express the choice (e.g.,
    the notebook has no sources).

### 2. Handling "Start Over" & Card Abandonment

-   If a Questionnaire Card or Review Card is currently pending/unsubmitted in
    chat, and the user sends a message indicating they want to start over, try
    again, or create a different video (e.g., "generate a new video", "start
    over", "start again", "make another video", "new video", "let's try again",
    "scratch that"):
    -   **Treat the previous card as ABANDONED.**
    -   **PURGE all previous selections**: Discard all prior format choices,
        focus chips, topic titles, and style selections from the abandoned card.
        **Never carry forward abandoned preferences.**
    -   **Evaluate the new request as fresh**:
        -   If the user provided a specific new topic (e.g., "start over and
            make a video on photosynthesis"), gather context for that new topic
            and present Step 0 or Step 1 for it.
        -   If the user did NOT provide a topic (e.g., just "generate a new
            video", "start over"), the request is underspecified — **you MUST
            present Step 0: Questionnaire Card**. Never skip Step 0 by recycling
            the abandoned topic!
    -   **Never call `create_artifact`**: An abandoned card must never trigger
        generation.

## Translation & Localization (CRITICAL)

All human-facing display strings across both QuestionnaireCard and
CoCreationReviewCard A2UI components MUST be translated into the user's active
device/conversation language (e.g., Spanish, French, German, Japanese, etc.).

### What MUST be translated into the user's active language:

-   **Card Titles**: e.g., `"Let's set up your video"`, `"Video: <Topic>"`
-   **Question Text & Subtitles**: e.g., `"What should the format be?"`, `"What
    should the video focus on?"`, `"Select 1 or 2 topics for a sharper video"`
-   **Option Labels & Descriptions**: e.g., `"Explainer"`, `"Comprehensive
    overview that connects the dots"`, `"Short"`, `"Bite-sized overview to help
    quickly grasp core ideas"`, `"Cinematic"`, `"Engaging, expressive content
    that dives deep"`
-   **Focus Chip Labels**: Dynamic and pre-selected focus topics
-   **Review Notice Text**: Title, label, and expanded label (e.g., `"Review
    producer notes"`, `"Review producer notes before final rendering"`, `"Refine
    draft producer notes before final generation..."`)
-   **Any other human-readable display strings** presented to the user in the
    UI.

### What MUST NOT be translated (Preserve structural identifiers):

-   Schema keys and property names (e.g., `surfaceId`, `catalogId`, `component`,
    `id`, `icon`, `imageEnum`, `selectionType`, `subtitle`,
    `subtitleVisibleOptions`, `options`, `questions`, `styleList`,
    `selectedStyle`, `styleVisibleFormats`, `reviewNotice`)
-   Structural IDs and enum values (e.g., `"root"`, `"QuestionnaireCard"`,
    `"CoCreationReviewCard"`, `"explainer"`, `"short"`, `"cinematic"`,
    `"crop_16_9"`, `"crop_9_16"`, `"movie"`, `"stylus_note_spark"`,
    `"subscriptions"`, `"vo_styles"`, `"auto_select"`, `"en"`, `"es"`, `"fr"`,
    `"de"`, `"ja"`, `"ko"`, `"pt"`, `"zh"`, etc.)

> **OVERRIDE NOTICE:** This Translation & Localization clause overrides any
> directive to copy text in quotes as-is. While structural identifiers, keys,
> IDs, icons, and enums must be preserved as-is, all human-readable display
> strings must be translated into the active device/conversation language.

## Step 0: Co-Creation Questionnaire Card (Conditional)

Decide using the **whole active journey**, not just the latest message. If the
user is answering a question you asked, read the answer together with their
original request.

After reading the journey, you know…                                                                                                      | Next step
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------
Which angle, theme, historical arc, or section to cover (e.g., "bioluminescence in the deep sea", "how X changed over time", "chapter 3") | Step 1: Review Card
Only the broad notebook subject, or nothing yet (e.g., "make me a video")                                                                 | Step 0: Questionnaire Card

-   **At most one chat question per journey.** Once the user has answered it,
    your next reply is a card.
-   These cards are this skill's planning step. Don't also propose a plan in
    chat.
-   Introduce the card with one short sentence, without citations.
-   Abandoned journeys don't count as context. See **Handling "Start Over"**.

### Requirements

Every field within the "focus" section **must** have a thoughtfully pre-selected
default based on your context gathering above.

#### Focus Chips Guidelines

-   **Quantity**: Generate **3-5 distinct focus chips** (always generate at
    least 3 chips) derived from source content. Having 3–5 options provides
    users with a diverse range of angles to explore and prevents jamming
    multiple topics into single chips. Pre-select 1–2 with the richest source
    grounding.
-   **Single Topic Per Chip (CRITICAL)**: Each focus chip MUST represent
    strictly ONE coherent concept, angle, or theme. The topics chosen must be
    the most compelling or representative of the source's content, with
    sufficient substance to support a narrative without being too narrowly
    focused.
    -   **NEVER combine or link multiple disparate topics into a single chip.**
    -   **Do NOT use '&', 'and', '+', '/', 'or', hyphens, or commas to join two
        distinct concepts** (e.g., do NOT generate "Global Logistics & Equipment
        Transport" or "Sustainability & Net Zero 2030"; split them into separate
        chips like "Global logistics", "Equipment transport", "Sustainability
        goals", "Net-zero by 2030"). Hyphenated words like "net-zero" are fine.
    -   If source material covers multiple related areas, create separate,
        distinct chips for each individual topic.
-   **Succinct Phrasing**: Keep chips concise and human-digestible: **3 to 6
    words**, ideally 4 to 6, on a single continuous line. Ensure suggestions are
    expressive and compelling (e.g., "How noise cancelling works", "Why ice is
    slippery", "Physics behind ski edges", "Tesla's rivalry with Edison", "5
    moments from Google I/O") rather than overly terse or dry topic labels
    (avoid clipped labels like "Economic impact"). Avoid introductory articles
    ("The ..."), filler words, or wordy academic phrasing (prefer "Physics
    behind ski edges" over "The Physics Behind Contemporary Ski Edges").
-   **Prompt Formatting**: Each focus chip's label MUST follow a clear sentence
    pattern:
    -   `'How [subject] [verb]'` (e.g., `'How noise cancelling works'`)
    -   `'Why [surprising claim]'` (e.g., `'Why ice is slippery'`)
    -   `'[Noun phrase] of/behind [subject]'` (e.g., `'Physics behind ski
        edges'`)
    -   Descriptive noun phrase (e.g., `'Knit and purl basics'`, `'Street
        circuit dynamics'`)
    -   `'[Subject]'s [dramatic noun phrase]'` (e.g., `"Tesla's rivalry with
        Edison"`)
    -   `'[Number] [things] from [source]'` (e.g., `'5 moments from Google
        I/O'`)
-   Use sentence case (capitalize only the first word and proper nouns).
-   Use concrete nouns and active verbs — name the specific subject, not a
    category.

#### Focus Chips Negative Constraints

-   **Do NOT combine multiple topics into a single chip** (no '&', 'and', '+',
    '/', 'or', hyphens, or commas joining distinct concepts). Hyphenated words
    like "net-zero" are fine.
-   **Do NOT exceed 6 words per chip.** Keep chips concise and expressive (4–6
    words preferred).
-   **Do NOT start suggestions with imperative verbs** like Explain, Describe,
    Create, Generate, or Summarize. Frame the suggestion as a noun phrase or
    question-form topic (e.g., 'How X works' rather than 'Explain X'). The
    prompt should read as a topic label, not a command.
-   **Do NOT use colons or multi-clause sentences.**
-   **Do NOT use multi-line formatting**, newlines, bullet points, or numbered
    lists. Each suggestion must be a single continuous line of text.
-   **Use numerals and symbols** instead of spelling out numbers and units
    (e.g., '18%' not 'eighteen percent', '$5M' not 'five million dollars', '3x'
    not 'three times') to keep suggestions compact.

### Questionnaire Card A2UI Structure

Every `<...>` field must be populated using context. For fields WITHOUT `<...>`,
preserve structural identifiers (`id`, `icon`, `selectionType`,
`subtitleVisibleOptions`) exactly as defined, but translate human-visible
display strings (`title`, `text`, `subtitle`, `label`, `description`) into the
active device/conversation language per the **Translation & Localization**
clause.

```json
[
  {
    "version": "v0.9",
    "createSurface": {
      "surfaceId": "<unique-surface-id>",
      "catalogId": "notebooklm:nlm_v1"
    }
  },
  {
    "version": "v0.9",
    "updateComponents": {
      "surfaceId": "<unique-surface-id>",
      "components": [
        {
          "id": "root",
          "component": "QuestionnaireCard",
          "title": "Let's set up your video",
          "questions": [
            {
              "id": "format",
              "icon": "movie",
              "text": "What should the format be?",
              "selectionType": "single",
              "options": [
                {
                  "id": "explainer",
                  "label": "Explainer",
                  "icon": "crop_16_9",
                  "selected": true,
                  "description": "Comprehensive overview that connects the dots"
                },
                {
                  "id": "short",
                  "label": "Short",
                  "icon": "crop_9_16",
                  "description": "Bite-sized overview to help quickly grasp core ideas"
                },
                {
                  "id": "cinematic",
                  "label": "Cinematic",
                  "icon": "crop_16_9",
                  "description": "Engaging, expressive content that dives deep"
                }
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "focus",
              "icon": "stylus_note_spark",
              "text": "What should the video focus on?",
              "subtitle": "Select 1 or 2 topics for a sharper video",
              "subtitleVisibleOptions": ["short"],
              "selectionType": "multi",
              "options": [
                {
                  "id": "focus-1",
                  "label": "<topic 1 from sources>",
                  "selected": true
                },
                {
                  "id": "focus-2",
                  "label": "<topic 2 from sources>",
                  "selected": true
                },
                {
                  "id": "focus-3",
                  "label": "<topic 3 from sources>"
                },
                {
                  "id": "focus-4",
                  "label": "<topic 4 from sources>"
                },
                {
                  "id": "focus-5",
                  "label": "<topic 5 from sources>"
                }
              ]
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  }
]
```

Wait for the user's response before proceeding.

## Step 1: Co-Creation Review Card

Present a **Co-Creation Review Card** summarizing everything before dispatching
a video generation. This gives the user a final chance to confirm or tweak
before generation begins.

### Step 0 → Step 1 Transition (if applicable)

A Questionnaire Card submission ends with a hidden
`<!-- a2ui-submitted: {...} -->` tag. Route on its `action` field — not on the
visible sentence, which is localized (if `action` is absent, treat `"surprise":
true` as Skip planning):

-   `"questionnaireCardSurprise"` (**Skip planning**): skip Step 1 and dispatch
    now with `enable_planning="false"`, mapping the tag's `format`/`focus` per
    the Step 2 parameter table and filling the rest from context.
-   `"questionnaireCardSubmit"` (**Continue**): build the Review Card. The tag
    lists only what the user **chose**; derive the rest from the Questionnaire
    Card you emitted earlier in the conversation: any chip you offered that is
    absent from the submission was **deselected**, and any submitted chip you
    did not offer was **typed by the user**. **You MUST carry these forward** as
    defaults in the Review Card:

-   Set `selected: true` on the matching `format.options` entry.
-   Synthesize `focusDescription` **only** from the selected focus chips. The
    selected chips define the subject; source material may supply supporting
    sub-points *within* that subject, but must never introduce an additional
    subject.

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> If the user came from Step 0 and already chose a format or focus areas, those
> selections **must** be reflected as defaults in the Review Card. The user
> should not have to re-select anything they already chose.

### Accompanying Turn Message (Chat)

When presenting the Co-Creation Review Card:

-   Provide brief context on what is happening during this turn (e.g., "I've set
    up a review card for you to confirm your final options before kicking off
    generating your video.").
-   **Do NOT explain a lengthy narrative arc, outline, or scene breakdown in the
    chat.** Keep your accompanying chat message to 1–2 concise, friendly
    sentences.

### Dynamic Field Population Rules

Every `<...>` field must be populated using context. For fields WITHOUT `<...>`,
preserve structural identifiers (`id`, `imageEnum`, `styleList`) exactly as
defined, but translate human-visible display strings (`title`, `text`, `label`,
`description`) into the active device/conversation language per the
**Translation & Localization** clause.

Field               | How to Populate
------------------- | ---------------
`title`             | Format: `"Video: <Topic>"`. Derive the topic from: (1) the user's last message (highest priority), (2) Step 0 focus selections, (3) source material's main theme. Keep it concise — 3–6 words. Avoid generic titles like "Video: Overview".
`format.selected`   | Set `selected: true` on the option that matches: (1) the user's Step 0 selection, (2) explicit mention in conversation (e.g., "short video"), (3) default to `"explainer"` only if no signal exists.
`language.selected` | Set `selected: true` on the option that matches: (1) the user's explicit language preference (e.g., "make it in Spanish"), (2) the dominant language of the source material, (3) default to `"en"` (English) if no signal exists.
`style.selected`    | Set `selectedStyle` to the style ID that best matches the content's tone. Available IDs: `"auto_select"` (default/general), `"classic"` (scientific/technical/professional), `"whiteboard"` (educational/instructional), `"watercolor"` (nature/atmospheric/artistic), `"retro_print"` (vintage/historical/editorial), `"heritage"` (cultural/traditional), `"papercraft"` (playful/crafty/DIY), `"anime"` (pop culture/entertainment/dynamic), `"kawaii"` (c

articles.title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio
articles.description: OpenAI is acquiring Orchestra Bio to bring AI-powered operations to life sciences R&D, helping biopharma teams accelerate drug development and advance new treatments.
articles.full_text:
Title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/openai-to-acquire-orchestra-bio

Markdown Content:
OpenAI has acquired [Orchestra Bio⁠(opens in a new window)](https://orchestra.bio/), a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. We’re bringing Orchestra’s team and technology together with [Rosalind](https://openai.com/rosalind/), our AI models and tools for life sciences research. Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner.

Developing a new medicine is extraordinarily complex, taking roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery to regulatory approval in the United States. Beyond the science, teams must orchestrate programs across internal departments and external partners, often relying on disconnected systems. We’re now at an inflection point where AI can help take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows.

## Bringing Rosalind and Orchestra together

[Rosalind](https://openai.com/rosalind/) brings our AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. [GPT‑Rosalind](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-rosalind/) helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. [Rosalind Workbench⁠](https://openai.com/rosalind/#product) connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data to help researchers analyze results and plan experiments.

Orchestra brings a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine.

## Designed for the way biopharma teams work

Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, freeing up time to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays.

A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. A failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents help teams identify which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next.

Realizing the potential of AI in life sciences requires close collaboration with the organizations working at the forefront of drug discovery and development. Our partnership with [Novo Nordisk⁠](https://openai.com/rosalind/#novo-nordisk) aims to translate its scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance. At [Moderna⁠](https://openai.com/rosalind/#moderna), AI is helping teams translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D.

Our vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines: exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that vision. Alongside researchers and our partners, we aim to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

articles.title: Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages
articles.description: Learn how OpenAI is improving ChatGPT across low-resource programming languages, with new evaluations for software engineering, SQLite, and COBOL migration.
articles.full_text:
Title: Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/low-resource-programming-languages

Markdown Content:
Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL [supports⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/cobol) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in [weather forecasting⁠(opens in a new window)](https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/71120) and [nuclear reactor safety analysis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.nrc.gov/education-regulatory-research/research/computer-codes). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.

This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.

To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does.

Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.

On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost.

On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, nearly saturating the evaluation.

Together, these results show that our models are becoming significantly better at working with a wide range of programming languages, while also becoming more cost-efficient.

## 1. Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)

MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.

At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%). Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.

GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%. Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.

We are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on [GitHub⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/MultiLangBench), along with results for each language. Developers can inspect what the evaluation tests, review performance in the languages they use, and identify gaps that matter for their own work.

## 2. Migrating a COBOL codebase

Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

Successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.

To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.

On this evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT‑5.6 Sol’s 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation. These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.

## Advancing capabilities for enterprise software

These evaluations, alongside direct feedback from developers and enterprise customers, help us see where our models are improving and where they still fall short.

Our goal is to help models apply software engineering skills across more languages: understanding unfamiliar repositories, planning changes, using build tools, running tests, and debugging failures.

You can try our latest models through the API on coding tasks in the languages your team uses. Your feedback on what works, where the models struggle, and which languages or workflows we should focus on next helps shape how we train and evaluate models to better support the software you depend on.

An update for builders using Codex on Windows:

We’ve built a new sandbox mode using @Microsoft’s Execution Containers (MXC) for faster setup, stronger network enforcement, and granular file access controls.

Requires a compatible Windows 11 device.

quoted_tweet.author: pavandavuluri
quoted_tweet.text:
Today, we announced new @Windows platform capabilities and @surface devices built to empower people and organizations for the era of hybrid intelligence. Here are some of the highlights:

- It all starts with trust. Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) is now generally available on Windows 11, keeping agents contained within boundaries the operating system enforces.

- HydraFusion brings hybrid intelligence to life, allowing models to run locally while seamlessly accessing the cloud when more scale or capability is needed. We're working with @github to extend HydraFusion to Windows.

- This fall, Search on the taskbar adds thousands of quick actions, making it easier to adjust settings and get things done as fast as you can type.

- @MSFTCopilot is getting more powerful on Windows. With hybrid intelligence, it can tap into your PC's local capabilities and turn your requests into action, while keeping you in control.

- Local agents are coming to Windows too. Muse is on its way as a native Windows app with MXC integration, and Hermes, OpenClaw, and Perplexity are already building local experiences on Windows.

- Surface Laptop Ultra, built with NVIDIA RTX Spark, is the most powerful Surface we've ever built. It's available for pre-order today, along with the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box and new RTX Spark PCs from our partners. Call of Duty is coming to RTX Spark in 2027.

Read more on the Windows Blog: https://t.co/DRx3HgDqsS

articles.description:
🚀 Meet Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo — create and edit images in just 8 denoising steps! Open weights now available!

Built on Qwen-Image-2.1, Turbo is an accelerated checkpoint on the same 7B visual generation architecture. 

Fewer steps does not mean lower quality: it still generates strong 2K images from text, and supports continued creation through natural-language edits, from adding accessories to changing a scene.

Start directly with Diffusers: load QwenImage21Pipeline and the checkpoint’s recommended 8-step sampling schedule is ready to go. 

🌐 Prefer an API? Qwen-Image-2.1 Pro and Turbo APIs are now officially live. Choose a hosted API for your application, or use the Turbo weights in your own workflow.

🤖 ModelScope:
https://t.co/Cixiro51v8
🤗 Hugging Face:
https://t.co/4GqXcYeAmB
🔗 Pro API:
https://t.co/fw2am7VCP7
🔗 Turbo API:
https://t.co/qmDvTqiVZK

What will you create with 8 steps? Share your results with us!

quoted_tweet.author: Alibaba_Qwen
quoted_tweet.text:
Meet Qwen-Image-2.1, the most balanced and cost-effective image generation model in the Qwen-Image series! Now open weights! 🎨

A unified model for both generation and editing, delivering top-tier quality in a lightweight package.

Highlights: 👀
- Compact & exceptionally fast: A lightweight 7B architecture that outperforms most closed-source models, with drastically accelerated inference for multi-image inputs.
- Native transparency: Natively generates and edits RGBA layers, enabling seamless compositing and text editing within transparent images.
- Versatile, high-fidelity editing: Supports up to 10 reference images and precise local control while preserving strict fidelity for portraits and products.
- Broad coverage & stunning aesthetics: Excels at panoramas, infographics, and virtual try-ons, delivering realistic textures and elegant typography.

Start to create your next masterpiece with Qwen-Image-2.1! 🖼️
